template.name: Psychiatric Diagnostic Evaluation & Clinical Note Master
template.description: Standardized clinical documentation template for psychiatric diagnostic evaluations, intake encounters, and clinical therapy add-on notes. Converts raw clinical intake notes, patient dialogues, and collateral interviews into a structured, audit-ready medical record with Chief Complaint, HPI, Meds, Psych Hx, ROS, MSE, Numbered Assessment, and Psychotherapy Add-on Plan.
template.formatRules:
Follow this exact clinical section order, exact capitalization, spacing, and punctuation:

CHIEF COMPLAINT: - [Primary diagnoses / chief concerns, e.g. MDD, Age related cognitive decline]
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: -
[Comprehensive continuous narrative paragraph in objective third-person medical phrasing ("The client is a...", "The patient reports..."). Detail age, referral/intake reason, accompanied collateral, precipitating life events, timeline, environmental triggers, subjective symptom endorsements (sadness, crying episodes, sleep disruption, appetite decline), fall history, acute medical co-morbidities (e.g. UTI, constipation), cognitive recall, and collateral history provided by family members or caregivers.]

CURRENT PSYCH MEDICATIONS: - [List psychotropic medications or None]

CURRENT NON-PSYCH MEDICATIONS: - 
- [List each non-psychiatric medication with bullet points or None]

PAST PSYCH MEDICATIONS: - [List past psychiatric medications or None]

PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: - [Document prior depressive episodes, outpatient therapy, psychiatric hospitalizations, or Denies]

SUBSTANCE ABUSE HISTORY: - [Tobacco, alcohol, illicit substance use history, cessation history, or Denies]

Trauma Hx: [Document trauma history or None]

SOCIAL HISTORY/ EDUCATIONAL HX: - [Birthplace, family, military/employment history, marriage duration/bereavement, relocations, snowbird history, local support system, hobbies, isolation factors]

Legal Hx: - [Document legal history or None]

FAMILY PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: - [Family mental health history or Denies]

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: - [General medical conditions, acute illnesses, e.g. UTI, constipation, falls]

DRUG ALLERGY: - 
- [List all documented drug allergies with bullet points or NKDA]

Objective:
Vital Signs: Height: Weight: (Pounds), BP: Pulse: Resp: 

 O: REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: 
Constitutional: [Constitutional ROS findings]
EYE: [Ophthalmologic ROS findings]
CARDIOVASCULAR: [Cardiovascular ROS findings]
RESPIRATORY: [Respiratory ROS findings]
GASTROINTESTINAL: [Gastrointestinal ROS findings, e.g. constipation treated with suppositories]
Endocrine: [Endocrine ROS findings]
MUSCULO-SKELETAL: [Musculoskeletal ROS findings, mobility limitations, assistive devices]
NEUROLOGICAL: [Orientation, headache, confusion, seizures, balance]

Mental Status Exam:
- Appearance: [Age-appropriate appearance, assistive devices, sensory aids]
- Behavior: [Cooperative, engaged, anxiety level at onset]
- Speech: [Clarity, coherence, spontaneity, rate]
- Mood: [Subjective mood description]
- Affect: [Affective range, congruence, tearfulness, brightening with positive topics]
- Thought Process: [Linear, goal-directed]
- Thought Content: [Focus of thought, grief, adjustment, explicit denial of suicidal or homicidal ideation]
- Cognition: [Orientation status, short-term memory, long-term recall]
- Insight: [Good / Fair / Poor]
- Judgment: [Good / Fair / Poor]

Assessment: 
    1. [Numbered prioritized clinical recommendations, medication continuations, weekly monitoring check-ins, grief normalization, family caregiving dynamics, fall prevention measures, and medical co-management.]

Plan
Psychosocial/ Psychotherapeutic/ Behavioral Assessment (Therapy Add-on only): 

Type of therapy used: [] Motivational interviewing [] CBT [x] Supportive therapy 

Intervention: [Document therapy intervention utilized, e.g. Supportive therapy]

Total psychotherapy time: - [Duration in minutes, e.g. 59 minutes]

Target Symptoms: [Primary target symptoms addressed during therapy]
Description: [Detailed clinical description of psychotherapeutic exploration, psychoeducation on adjustment/grief, exploration of support systems, and family counseling]

Goal/Progress: [Summary of session goals and patient response]
Treatment Goals: [x] decrease depressive sx [x] decrease anxiety sx [] decrease conflicts/ anger [] decrease psychosis [] decrease confusion [x] improve coping skills [] reduce negative bx [X] improve treatment compliance [] improve focus and attention [x] increase motivation [] decrease mood volatility [x] Improve sleep patterns [] decrease alcohol consumption [] decrease marijuana use [] decrease substance use
Treatment Goals Measured by: [x] decrease episodes of emotional/ behavioral problems [x] improved compliance with treatment [] decrease need for PRN medications [x] positive interactions with peers/family [ x] increased participation in interactions [] Increased focus and energy [x ] Increased motivation [x] Healthy sleep patterns [x] Healthy eating patterns [] decreased mood volatility [ ] decreased alcohol consumption [ ] decreased marijuana use [] decreased substance use
Progress Related to Goals: [] good [] fair [] minimal [x] assess at f/u
Functional Status: [] good [x] fair [] poor
Interactive Complexity (only use when therapy is coded): [] Maladaptive communication: [] cognitive deficits [] memory impaired [] limited insight [] repeated questions [] distractible [] argumentative [] denial of symptoms [] hearing impaired [] Caregiver/ Family Emotions or Behavior  
Prognosis: [] good [] fair [x] guarded [] poor
Disposition: Continue with follow-up care.
- Discussed diagnosis, treatment, risks benefits side effects, and alternate treatment.
- Medication, their effects, and side effects including metabolic, EPS, effect on the heart were discussed.
- Risk of medication increases with substance abuse and drinking. Compliance was addressed.
RETURN TO CLINIC: [ 4] Week(s) [] Month(s) [] PRN
template.editRules:
1. Transform raw psychiatric intake notes, conversational transcripts, or clinical summaries into a rigorous, third-person medical record ("The client is a...", "The patient reports...", "He states...").
2. Accurately separate psychotropic medications (CURRENT PSYCH MEDICATIONS) from general medical treatments (CURRENT NON-PSYCH MEDICATIONS).
3. Explicitly itemize all documented drug allergies under DRUG ALLERGY: - (e.g. Amoxicillin, Sulfamethoxazole/Trimethoprim) and highlight reported severe adverse reactions.
4. Integrate collateral history from family members, case managers, or caregivers into HPI and the Psychotherapy Add-on plan with exact attribution.
5. In Assessment, synthesize clinical decisions into a clean sequentially numbered list (1, 2, 3...) covering medication continuity, weekly monitoring check-ins, grief normalization, family dynamics, and fall prevention.
6. Populate the Psychotherapy Add-on checklist with precise brackets ([x] for checked/active items, [] for unchecked items) across Treatment Goals, Measures, Progress, Functional Status, and Prognosis.
7. Preserve all clinical metrics, numbers, dates, ages, and medical details without hallucination or truncation.
template.masterPrompt: You are an elite board-certified psychiatric documentation specialist. Transform raw patient encounter notes, clinical summaries, or intake transcripts into a standardized, audit-proof psychiatric diagnostic evaluation. Adhere strictly to the required section headers, Review of Systems, Mental Status Exam, numbered Assessment items, and Psychotherapy Add-on checklist. Return only the clinical document conforming to the formatting contract.

outputGuide.title: Psychiatric Diagnostic Evaluation Standard
outputGuide.description: Clinical documentation standards for psychiatric evaluations, Review of Systems, Mental Status Examination, and psychotherapy add-on records.
outputGuide.speakerFormat: Standardized medical record section headers (e.g., 'CHIEF COMPLAINT: -', 'HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: -', 'CURRENT PSYCH MEDICATIONS: -').
outputGuide.paragraphRules: Single comprehensive narrative block for HPI; categorized lists for medications and allergies; numbered entries for Assessment; bracketed checklist for Therapy Add-on.
outputGuide.punctuationRules: Standard medical documentation punctuation. Bullet points for medication lists and ROS categories.
outputGuide.uncertaintyMarkers: Record unknown dosages or unconfirmed strengths as reported; note patient uncertainty regarding exact dates or years.
outputGuide.editorialNotes: Clinical third-person voice. Precise separation of psychiatric vs non-psychiatric medications and strict allergy documentation.

checks.label: Clinical Section Headers Integrity
checks.description: Verifies all required psychiatric sections are present in standard sequence.
checks.rule: Standard section headers (CHIEF COMPLAINT, HPI, MEDICATIONS, ROS, MSE, Assessment, Plan).

checks.label: Medication & Allergy Separation
checks.description: Ensures psych and non-psych medications are cleanly categorized and drug allergies are itemized.
checks.rule: Separate CURRENT PSYCH, NON-PSYCH, and DRUG ALLERGY sections.

checks.label: Review of Systems & MSE Completeness
checks.description: Validates standard Review of Systems organ systems and complete Mental Status Exam fields.
checks.rule: Complete ROS and 10 MSE fields (Appearance, Behavior, Speech, Mood, Affect, Thought Process, Thought Content, Cognition, Insight, Judgment).

checks.label: Numbered Assessment List
checks.description: Ensures assessment items are sequentially numbered with concrete management steps.

checks.label: Psychotherapy Add-on Checklist & Return to Clinic

checks.rule: Checkbox format [x] / [] and RETURN TO CLINIC designation.

template.sampleInput:
Dothy is a 96-year-old female presenting for an initial psychiatric evaluation, accompanied by her son John. The primary concern is depressive symptoms and emotional distress in the context of recent major life changes, including the death of her husband of nearly 60 years (just before Christmas) and a permanent relocation to Arizona approximately three weeks ago. Dothy's mood is notably low, particularly in relation to grief over her husband and the emotional weight of returning to a place she and her husband visited together for 13 winters. She denies suicidal or homicidal ideation. Mood and anxiety are not formally rated on a numeric scale during this visit, though Dothy endorses sadness, episodes of crying (particularly when reminded of her husband), and emotional heaviness associated with her new living situation. She reports sleeping has been disrupted over the past week due to a recent urinary tract infection (UTI), waking around 4:00 AM, but reports generally sleeping adequately prior to the infection. Appetite is poor, which she attributes both to her age (96) and the current UTI, noting she does not feel hungry and eats very little. She reports eating better when her daughter Melinda was present, as Melinda prepared foods she enjoyed, such as tacos. Dothy's goal, as expressed during the session, is to feel better emotionally and to adjust to her new living environment, with the support of her family.
Dothy describes feeling sad since moving to her current residence, which she identifies as a place she and her late husband visited together for 13 consecutive winters over approximately 33 years. She states, "I think being here makes me sad because we used to come here about 13 times." She notes that a male resident in the facility strongly reminds her of her late husband - the resident uses a wheelchair, has lost the use of his legs, and has difficulty controlling his hands while eating, which mirrors how her husband appeared during his illness. She states, "When I see this guy, he looks almost like my husband," and identifies this as a daily emotional trigger. She reports crying episodes, particularly when talking about her husband or listening to music. She states she only cries when reminded of her husband and denies crying at other times.
When asked about daily functioning, Dothy reports she is on a walker and has limited mobility, which restricts her activities. She acknowledges a decline in interest in hobbies since turning 96 but does not endorse a complete loss of interest in life. She expresses anticipation about seeing friends when her daughter Melinda visits the following Thursday, including a friend from her Sweet Adelines/barbershop singing group who now lives locally but is confined to her home due to heart problems, and another friend in a nearby city. She does not feel her life is empty, stating, "I got my daughter." She identifies herself as a social person and expresses a desire to engage socially, though she has not yet initiated activities at the facility. She states she does not want to "sit in a chair and look out the window."
Dothy reports two recent falls: one approximately 10 days ago when the bathroom door got caught under her walker, and another when she over-lifted her lift chair and slipped, falling on her face. She now leaves the bathroom door open to prevent recurrence and no longer over-lifts the chair.
She reports a recent UTI and associated constipation, for which she received suppositories. She believes the constipation may have contributed to the UTI. She reports getting hot and cold with the infection and waking around 4:00 AM over the past week.
Dothy denies ever forgetting who she is or where she is. She acknowledges some short-term memory decline consistent with aging, stating, "A lot of things I remember them, but then there's things that I don't remember." Long-term memory appears intact, as evidenced by detailed recall of her life history, travels, and relationships. She correctly identifies her name, birth date (9/8/1939), the current month (September), and notes she just celebrated her 96th birthday two days prior. She is uncertain of the exact year but approximates it as 2026.
Dothy denies feeling lonely, helpless, or that her life is empty. She affirms that she is basically satisfied with her life and that it is wonderful to be alive. She does not report dreams. She denies wanting to be left alone. She acknowledges that she misses her husband more since arriving in Arizona than she did while in North Carolina, stating, "I think I miss my husband more since up here than in North Carolina."
Son John provides collateral history, noting that Dothy has been exhibiting signs consistent with depression since the move - increased sadness, reluctance to socially engage, and episodes of extreme crying. He notes she has always had some difficulty socializing but that current presentation is more pronounced. He also describes a longstanding pattern of dependency, noting that Dothy has rarely been alone for extended periods throughout her life - she was raised with her mother and sisters, married for nearly 60 years, and for the past 15 years (and especially the past two years), her daughter Melinda has been her primary caregiver, managing all aspects of daily life including making coffee, turning on lights, and assisting with internet tasks. John notes that Melinda moved in with their parents and took on a full caregiving role, particularly as both parents aged. John expresses concern about the current caregiving dynamic, noting that he and Melinda have had significant conflict over the level of involvement expected, with Melinda advocating for 24/7 presence and John feeling this is unsustainable. He requests guidance on how to support Dothy's transition while also addressing the family dynamic.
---
**Social History**
Dothy was born and raised in Iowa, where she and her husband raised their two children, John and Melinda. She describes having a good life in Iowa. She later lived in Jacksonville, Florida, where she worked as a dental hygienist and met her husband, who was in military service. She and her husband were married for nearly 60 years until his death just before Christmas of the prior year. They relocated to North Carolina around 2008 to be closer to their son John, who had moved there for employment. For approximately 33 years, Dothy and her husband were snowbirds, spending 13 winters in Arizona, typically arriving after Christmas and New Year's and staying approximately three months. Dothy permanently relocated to Arizona approximately three weeks ago following her husband's death. Her daughter Melinda has lived in Arizona for approximately 30 years and resides three miles from the facility. Her son John and his wife live in New Hampshire and are currently visiting. Dothy has a sister who is 98 years old and lives nearby; they have not yet reconnected. Dothy was previously involved in Sweet Adelines, a barbershop-style singing group, and describes herself as a social person. She reports having friends in the area whom she plans to visit when Melinda returns. She notes that in North Carolina, she and her husband felt socially isolated, as neighbors did not reach out to them, referring to them as "Yankees." She reports no current hobbies of note, attributing this to age and physical limitations.
---
**Past Psychiatric History**
Dothy has a history of mild depression, for which she was prescribed Mirtazapine by her primary care physician in North Carolina. She has been on this medication for several years. The exact onset of treatment is unclear but described as "quite a while ago." No prior psychiatric hospitalizations are mentioned. No prior formal therapy is documented.
---
**Legal History**

No legal history reported.
--
**Substance Use History**
Dothy reports a history of tobacco use in her 20s. She quit smoking after her daughter, at approximately 6 years old, encouraged her to stop, citing health concerns. She states quitting was not easy. No current tobacco use. No alcohol or illicit drug use reported or mentioned. Caffeine use not discussed.
---
**Objective**
Dothy is a 96-year-old female who presents as alert and oriented to person, place, and approximate time (knows her name, current location, and month/season; uncertain of exact year). She is cooperative and engaged throughout the session. She is accompanied by her son John, who provides collateral history. She uses a walker for ambulation and wears bilateral hearing aids, which she notes are difficult to insert and required adjustment during the session. She appears mildly anxious at the start of the visit, as noted by her son ("she might be a little nerved out"), but becomes more relaxed and conversational as the session progresses.
Dothy's tone throughout the session is warm, reflective, and at times emotionally tender, particularly when discussing her late husband. She becomes tearful when recounting memories of her husband and the emotional weight of returning to Arizona without him. Her energy level is low but appropriate for her age. She engages with humor at times and demonstrates good long-term recall, sharing detailed stories about her life, career, marriage, and travels. Her affect is congruent with her mood - predominantly sad when discussing her husband and the current transition, but brightening when discussing her daughter, friends, and plans for social engagement. She is future-oriented in some respects, expressing anticipation about upcoming visits with friends. She does not appear hopeless or despondent globally, but rather situationally grieving. Speech is clear and coherent. Thought process is linear and goal-directed. No evidence of psychosis, paranoia, or disorganized thinking. Short-term memory mildly impaired per self-report and collateral, consistent with age-related decline. Long-term memory intact.
Vital Signs: Not documented during this visit.
Mental Status Examination:
- Appearance: Age-appropriate, uses walker, bilateral hearing aids
- Behavior: Cooperative, engaged, mildly anxious at onset
- Speech: Clear, coherent, spontaneous
- Mood: Sad, grieving, situationally depressed
- Affect: Congruent, tearful at times, brightens with positive topics
- Thought Process: Linear, goal-directed
- Thought Content: Focused on grief, adjustment to new living situation, memories of husband; denies suicidal or homicidal ideation
- Cognition: Oriented x3 (person, place, month/season); short-term memory mildly impaired per age; long-term memory intact
- Insight: Good
- Judgment: Good
---
**Medications and Diagnoses**
Medications:
- Mirtazapine - dosage documented as "one and a half tablets" per available records; exact milligram strength not confirmed during visit; taken orally for depression
- Blood pressure medication - name and dosage not specified
- Suppositories - recently prescribed for constipation; name and dosage not specified
- Antibiotics - currently being treated for UTI; specific antibiotic not named
Allergies:
- Amoxicillin (confirmed reaction - patient reports severe illness when administered despite reporting allergy)
- Sulfa/Sulfur medications

Diagnoses (per this visit):
- Acute Adjustment Disorder with depressed mood, in the context of bereavement and relocation
- Grief reaction following death of spouse
---
**Assessment**
1. Diagnosis: Acute Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood
Dothy presents with depressive symptoms including sadness, episodes of crying, social withdrawal, and emotional distress arising in direct response to multiple significant life stressors occurring within the past several months: the death of her husband of nearly 60 years just before Christmas, and a permanent relocation to Arizona approximately three weeks ago. Symptoms are situational and contextually driven. She does not meet criteria for major depressive disorder based on current presentation. She retains interest in social engagement, expresses future-oriented thinking, denies hopelessness globally, and affirms satisfaction with life. The adjustment disorder is compounded by the fact that her current residence is a location strongly associated with her late husband, and a fellow resident serves as a daily visual reminder of her husband's final illness.
2. Diagnosis: Bereavement / Grief Reaction
Dothy is actively grieving the loss of her husband of nearly 60 years. She reports that being in Arizona intensifies her grief compared to when she was in North Carolina, as this location holds strong shared memories. She identifies specific triggers including the fellow resident who resembles her husband and music. Grief is expressed through crying, sadness, and emotional heaviness. This is assessed as a normal, healthy grief response that is being complicated by environmental triggers and the abrupt nature of the relocation.
ICD and CPT Codes:
- F43.21 - Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood
- Z63.4 - Disappearance and Death of Family Member (Bereavement)
- Z60.3 - Acculturation Difficulty (relocation/transition)
- F32.A - Depression, Unspecified (underlying mild depression, longstanding, on Mirtazapine)
- CPT 90791 - Psychiatric Diagnostic Evaluation (Initial psychiatric evaluation, this visit)
- CPT 90837 - Psychotherapy, 60 minutes (if applicable for this initial visit)
---
**Plan**
1. Acute Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood
- Weekly visits by the provider to the facility to monitor mood, sleep, appetite, and overall adjustment
- Each visit will include brief check-ins on sleep quality, eating, pain, constipation, urinary symptoms, and emotional state, as these physical factors disproportionately affect mood in elderly patients
- Psychoeducation provided to Dothy and her son John regarding acute adjustment disorder - explained as a situational condition triggered by loss, relocation, and life changes, lasting approximately three to six months, which may manifest as sadness, loneliness, frustration, or anxiety
- No formal psychotherapy indicated at this time beyond supportive weekly check-ins; provider assessed that Dothy does not require intensive therapy sessions
- Encourage gradual social engagement within the facility at Dothy's own pace; discourage passive isolation (e.g., sitting alone looking out the window)
- Family counseling component: provider to meet with Dothy's daughter Melinda upon her return (expected one week from today) to discuss the family caregiving dynamic, transition planning, and Melinda's own emotional needs
- Recommend a staggered visitation schedule for family: transition from daily visits to every-other-day visits; gradually reduce visit duration (e.g., from five hours to two hours) to support Dothy's independent acclimation to the facility while maintaining family connection
- Assess Melinda for her own adjustment and grief response at next visit; provider noted Melinda may benefit from individual support given her strong attachment and caregiving identity
2. Bereavement / Grief Reaction
- Normalize grief process with Dothy; reinforce that her emotional responses are healthy and expected
- Encourage continued discussion of her husband and memories as part of healthy grieving
- Acknowledge environmental triggers (the fellow resident who resembles her husband, the location itself) and validate their emotional impact
- Reinforce that life continues and that engagement with friends, family, and activities is part of healthy adjustment
- Monitor for worsening or complicated grief at weekly visits
3. Longstanding Mild Depression (on Mirtazapine)
- Continue current Mirtazapine regimen as prescribed; dosage to be confirmed with records
- No medication changes initiated at this visit
- Monitor response to medication in context of current stressors at weekly visits
4. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
- Currently being treated; monitor resolution of symptoms including nighttime waking, temperature dysregulation
- Note allergy to amoxicillin and sulfa medications - ensure treating providers are aware
5. Constipation
- Recently treated with suppositories; monitor bowel regularity
- Encourage adequate hydration and dietary intake as tolerated

6. Recent Falls (x2 in past 10 days)
- Bathroom door to remain open at all times to prevent walker entrapment
- Dothy instructed not to over-lift the lift chair; she reports compliance
- Monitor for additional fall events at weekly visits; assess need for further fall prevention interventions
7. Poor Appetite / Nutritional Concerns
- Monitor appetite and nutritional intake at weekly visits
- Noted that Dothy eats better when familiar/preferred foods are available; family encouraged to bring preferred foods when visiting as tolerated by facility
---
**Provider Interventions**
The provider conducted an initial psychiatric evaluation with Dothy, beginning with collateral history from her son John prior to Dothy's full engagement in the session. The provider oriented the session by gathering background on the circumstances of the move, the family dynamic, and the observed behavioral changes. The provider then transitioned to direct engagement with Dothy, asking open-ended and structured questions to assess mood, cognition, orientation, sleep, appetite, fall history, and social functioning. The provider administered an informal geriatric depression screening using yes/no questions addressing life satisfaction, activity engagement, feelings of emptiness, loneliness, helplessness, and appreciation for life. The provider gently prompted Dothy to elaborate on her emotional experiences, including her feelings about returning to Arizona, her memories of her husband, and the impact of the fellow resident who reminds her of him. The provider also facilitated a family discussion with John, providing psychoeducation about acute adjustment disorder and grief, and offering concrete guidance on transitioning the caregiving schedule. The provider identified Melinda as a secondary concern and committed to meeting with her upon her return.

Patient Response: Dothy responded openly and warmly to the provider's questions, becoming more relaxed as the session progressed. She shared detailed personal history, expressed her grief clearly, and demonstrated insight into her emotional state. She acknowledged feeling sad and missing her husband more in Arizona than in North Carolina, and identified specific triggers for her sadness. She responded positively to the provider's normalization of her grief and expressed understanding of the adjustment process. She affirmed her desire to remain socially engaged and expressed anticipation about upcoming plans with friends. John engaged actively in the family discussion, expressing relief at the provider's framing of the situation and requesting guidance on how to suport his mother and address the conflict with his sister.
---
**Psychotherapy**
Total psychotherapy time: 50 minutes - 1 hour (Initial Visit)
Target Symptoms: Depressed mood, grief reaction, social withdrawal, emotional distress related to bereavement and relocation, adjustment difficulties
Description: Supportive psychotherapy was provided during this initial psychiatric evaluation. The provider engaged Dothy in a warm, validating conversation exploring her emotional experiences, grief, and adjustment to her new living environment. Psychoeducation was provided to both Dothy and her son regarding acute adjustment disorder and the grief process. The provider normalized Dothy's emotional responses and reinforced healthy coping through social engagement and family connection. Family systems discussion was incorporated, addressing the caregiving dynamic and transition planning.
Goal/Progress: Initial visit - baseline established. Dothy demonstrates good insight, intact long-term cognition, and preserved social motivation. She is actively grieving and adjusting to a significant life transition. Goals include stabilization of mood, facilitation of social reintegration within the facility, normalization of grief, and family psychoeducation. Provider to follow up weekly. Melinda to be engaged in the next session upon her return.

---

**Short Term Goals**
- Dothy will begin to identify and engage in at least one social activity or interaction within the facility per week over the next 30 days
- Dothy will maintain regular sleep and eating patterns as the UTI resolves
- Family will implement a staggered visitation schedule to support Dothy's independent adjustment
- Provider will meet with Melinda within the next week to address family caregiving dynamics and Melinda's own emotional needs
- Dothy will continue to verbalize and process grief related to her husband's death in weekly sessions
**Long Term Goals**
- Dothy will demonstrate improved emotional adjustment to her new living environment within three to six months, with reduction in situational depressive symptoms
- Dothy will establish a social network and routine within the facility that provides meaningful engagement and reduces isolation
- Family will develop a sustainable, balanced caregiving schedule that supports Dothy's independence while maintaining family connection
- Melinda will be assessed and, if appropriate, referred for her own individual support to address grief and caregiver identity concerns
- Dothy will continue to grieve her husband in a healthy, adaptive manner, integrating her memories into her current life rather than being immobilized by them
